title: Canonicalize egress binding on GPU pool eviction to prevent cross-tenant request reuse
creator: Aisha Koneru
description:
Summary: Multiple customers reported transient cross-tenant DNS/egress anomalies after Dedicated GPU pool scale-downs. The pattern: scale-down (pool eviction) coincides with active long-lived sessions; shortly after, DNS responses or upstream connections associated with the evicted tenant are observed by different tenants in the same dedicated host. Impact: customer-facing production requests occasionally received incorrect DNS answers or wrong upstream session context, causing PII-like hostname leaks and request failures.

Observed behavior and repro: Repro at scale was flakey but consistent when the autoscaler evicted GPUs while several tens of long-lived inference connections (KV cache + keep-alive) existed. Repro steps: 1) Provision a 4-GPU dedicated pool with two tenants pinned; 2) Start long-lived inference sessions that maintain NAT/SNAT mappings and resolver caches; 3) Trigger scale-down by reducing pool target; 4) After eviction of one worker, issue requests from the other tenant and observe intermittent DNS resolution of hostnames owned by the evicted tenant and resumed upstream TLS sessions referencing prior connection metadata.

Root cause hypothesis: The eviction code path returns ephemeral egress artifacts (SNAT port allocations, resolver cache entries, egress-metadata labels) back to a shared allocator without clearing tenant ownership tags. A race between connection teardown and the egress reconciler means some bindings are recycled with stale tenant metadata. Additionally, the peering/dns-proxy layer applies a cached reply classifier that uses stale binding IDs to tag responses. The combination allows ephemeral ports or resolver entries to be associated with the wrong tenant for a short window during pool shrink.

Immediate mitigations performed: 1) Rolled out a hotfix that forces per-tenant ephemeral SNAT ranges on newly created dedicated pools to reduce blast radius; 2) Deployed a temporary conservative guard in the egress reconciler to delay reuse of bindings for 60s after eviction; 3) Invalidated resolver caches for impacted customers and coordinated customer notifications and postmortems. These reduced surface area but do not address the root cause.

Planned permanent fix (implementation plan): - Egress manager changes: canonicalize binding lifecycle by adding explicit state transitions for BOUND -> RETIRING -> RECLAIMED. On RETIRING, drain active flows and mark binding owner as stale in control plane; do not return to global allocator until RECLAIMED. - SNAT allocator: partition ephemeral ranges by tenant for dedicated pools and add owner metadata checks on allocation/assignment. - Resolver proxy: attach binding UUIDs to cache entries and validate owner UUID before serving cached replies. - Add reconciliation job: scan existing bindings across hosts, identify stale owner fields, and perform safe reclamation with audit logs. - Add unit and integration tests that simulate concurrent eviction + in-flight connections. - Add metrics/tracing (egress.binding_state, egress.reclaimed_conflicts) and alerting.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge feature behind feature-flag and deploy to staging with synthetic repro harness; 2) Canary to a single region dedicated fleet with low-traffic tenants for 48h and monitor egress.binding_state and customer symptom dashboards; 3) Expand canary to 25% of Dedicated clusters for 72h; 4) Full rollout gated on zero new cross-tenant incidents for 7d and automated reconciliation success.

Testing & QA: create unit tests for state transitions, integration tests driving scaledown scenarios, and chaos test to evict workers while replaying realistic keepalive traffic. Add post-deploy verification job to scan per-tenant SNAT ownership and resolver cache correctness.

Communication: triaged with SEs and customer success, actively communicating mitigation steps to impacted customers; scheduled customer postmortems for next week.

Follow-ups: 1) Explore making per-tenant SNAT default for all Dedicated pools; 2) Audit other reclaim paths (e.g., LB reassign) for similar metadata-stale risks; 3) Add runbook for rapid revert and cache invalidation in future incidents.
